scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kanyarkali is an agricultural festival dance primarily associated with the Nair castes of the Palakkad district in Kerala.
It is performed during the months of April and May, following the village fairs (Vela) and coinciding with Vishu celebrations.
Historically, it depicts the social customs and lives of various castes and tribes from medieval Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kanyarkali is a ritualistic performance conducted over three to four consecutive nights.
It is timed with the agricultural cycle and the Vishu festival.
The Purattu segments serve as a social commentary or historical record, depicting the interactions, reunions, and customs of medieval society.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance begins with Vattakali, a rhythmic circular dance performed by men around a central lamp in a nine-pillared square pandal.
Dancers move along the periphery while singers and musicians stay in the center.
This is followed by Purattu, which are dramatic sketches.
Watch for Vattakali, Purattu.

Formation: Circular dancing along the periphery of a square pandal around a central lamp.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical ensemble for Kanyarkali includes the Chenda (drum), Elatalam (cymbals), and Chengalam (gong).
During the Vattakali phase, the Maddalam drum is also used as an accompaniment.
Listen for the Chenda, Elatalam, Chengalam, Maddalam.

The sound is dominated by the percussive drive of the Chenda and Maddalam drums, punctuated by the sharp clanging of Elatalam cymbals and the resonance of the Chengalam gong. The vocalizations transition from rhythmic chants in the circular dance to dramatic, character-driven dialogue and songs in the farcical segments.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance takes place in a specially constructed square pandal with a roof supported by nine pillars, located in front of a temple.
A lighted lamp is placed in the center.
Costumes are highly variable; because each Purattu depicts a different caste or tribe, the dancers change attire to reflect the specific social group being represented.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While individual historical founders are not named, the Nair community of Alathur and Chittur are the traditional custodians.
A significant recent milestone was the debut of women performers at Kakkayur, marking a shift in the traditionally male-dominated practice.
The dance is specific to the Palakkad district, particularly the taluks of Alathur and Chittur.
Kanyarkali belongs to the folk-ritual traditions of Kerala.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Kanyarkali is a temple ritual performed in a consecrated pandal; the central lamp is a sacred focal point and the performance is tied to the Vishu festival and village temple fairs.
